representativeSnapshot.kind: THE GAP, MEASURED. `rg -ln 'user_news_preferences|user_news_subscriptions' supabase/` returns exactly TWO live consumers (`lib/news/feed-service.ts` and `__tests__/news/news-feed-schema-drift.test.ts`) plus documentation, and ZERO migrations - not in the 320-file active chain, not in `supabase/migrations/archive/`, not in `supabase/migrations_backup/`, not in any root-level SQL. No `CREATE TABLE` for either relation exists anywhere in this repository. `lib/database.types.ts` declares neither. THE FAILURE IS INVISIBLE IN A WAY THE OTHER FOUR ARE NOT: a missing TABLE does not empty a news-feed section, it silently downgrades the RANKING of every section, so a signed-in reader's subscribed topics and sources are simply never applied and the feed still renders and still looks healthy. `lib/news/feed-service.ts:225-288` (`getUserPreferenceData`) reads both tables through the CALLER'S client and both reads previously reported nothing at all, because the reporter fired only from a `catch` and PostgREST resolves an absent table as `{ data: null, error }` rather than throwing. The discover lane has already made the failure loud in code (`error` is now destructured, logged and reported through `reportMissingSchemaOnce`, and the section is marked degraded); this file is the half that makes it stop happening. No second reporting mechanism is added. WHY THIS FILE IS THE RIGHT SHAPE: it is the only one of DB-019's five gaps where the column contract is COMPLETE rather than partial, because the consumer is a single function with four selected columns, two filters, one `maybeSingle()` and one `Array.isArray` per column - so the shape is derived from the caller and not guessed.
representativeSnapshot.evidenceArtifact: executed:throwaway PostgreSQL 16.15 cluster (initdb + pg_ctl in a temp dir, destroyed on exit) with `auth.users`, `auth.uid()` and the anon/authenticated/service_role roles emulated. This file applied THREE times consecutively, all exiting 0. Post-state measured: both relations present with relkind='r'; the six consumer columns present; `user_news_preferences_user_id_key` present; RLS enabled AND forced on both; exactly 6 policies, one per command, all named and all scoped to `auth.uid() = user_id`; `anon` holds no SELECT on either table. BEHAVIOURAL, as two distinct signed-in identities plus anon: user A reads 1 own preference row and 2 own subscription rows; user B reads 0 rows (a clean zero, NOT a permission error); user B's read of user A's row returns 0 rows; user B's INSERT naming user A is REJECTED with `new row violates row-level security policy`; user B's unqualified UPDATE matches 0 rows and user A's topics are byte-unchanged afterwards; user A's own UPDATE and upsert are ACCEPTED; user A's DELETE is REJECTED with `permission denied for table`; `anon` is REJECTED with `permission denied for table`; a bad `subscription_type` is REJECTED by the CHECK; a duplicate subscription is REJECTED by the unique constraint. NOT a Supabase target, not a hosted project, not a chain replay, no `supabase db reset`, no `db push --include-all` (CP-051). Migration SHA-256 0d0002a36daa72ff72039718bc4657f61492750f614b6841fcf13b879db10e76.

assumptions: `user_id` MUST be UNIQUE on `user_news_preferences`, and that is a hard consequence of the consumer, not a preference. `lib/news/feed-service.ts:238-242` reads with `.eq('user_id', params.userId).maybeSingle()`. PostgREST's `maybeSingle()` returns `PGRST116` when more than one row matches, so a plain column would turn every signed-in reader's news request into an error the moment they had two preference rows. `constraint user_news_preferences_user_id_key unique (user_id)` therefore exists for the caller's sake, and the post-condition asserts it STRUCTURALLY by looking for a unique constraint whose definition names `user_id` rather than by re-listing it.

The post-condition's structural check on that unique constraint is what makes the file safe against the one failure that would be invisible: a `create table if not exists` against a table that already exists on a target with a DIFFERENT shape is a silent no-op, so a target carrying a non-unique `user_id` would keep it and every signed-in read would 500 forever. The check makes that target fail the apply instead.

`topics` and `preferred_sources` are `text[] NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}'::text[]`, not nullable. The consumer does `Array.isArray(preferences?.topics) ? preferences?.topics : []`, so a NULL column and an empty array are indistinguishable at the read - which means a nullable column would turn a MISSING preference into a SILENTLY EMPTY preference rather than a detectable absence, and the `maybeSingle()` on a table with no row already returns null. NOT NULL is what makes the two states separable.

`subscription_type` is CHECK-constrained to `('topic','source')` because the consumer's only other behaviour is to DISCARD the row. `lib/news/feed-service.ts:280-282` tests `=== 'topic'` and `=== 'source'`; any third value is read and dropped with no log and no effect. An unconstrained column would let a caller write a value that is silently invisible forever, which is precisely the silent-empty failure this file exists to close. Rejecting at write is the fail-closed direction. Measured: INSERTing `subscription_type='weekly_digest'` returned `ERROR: new row for relation "user_news_subscriptions" violates check constraint "user_news_subscriptions_type_check"`.

`UNIQUE (user_id, subscription_type, subscription_key)` is the real intent of a subscription table and is not decoration. Subscribing to a topic twice must be idempotent; without the constraint a repeated write inserts a duplicate row, and the feed then folds the list into a `Set`, so the duplicate is INVISIBLE at the read and PERMANENT in the table - a drift that no test would ever see. Measured: a duplicate insert returned `duplicate key value violates unique constraint "user_news_subscriptions_unique_key"`.

`subscription_key` is stored AS WRITTEN and lowercased only at read (`String(subscription.subscription_key).toLowerCase()` at the consumer). Normalising on write would make an unsubscribe against the caller's original casing miss, and the stored value is what a future unsubscribe needs in order to match.

`id`, `created_at` and `updated_at` are added and are NOT invented product columns: nothing in the consumer reads them. They exist because a preference table with no surrogate key and no timestamps cannot be written to safely by any future caller and cannot be audited. Nothing else is added - no `frequency`, no `digest_enabled`, no `notification_channel` - because a preference column nobody asked for is a product surface this task's charter excludes.

AUTHORIZATION IS FAIL-CLOSED AND OWN-ROWS-ONLY, SERVER-SIDE. Both tables are read through the caller's own `SupabaseClient`, never a service-role client, so RLS is the only boundary. Every USING and every WITH CHECK is `auth.uid() = user_id`; there is no permissive policy, no `to anon` and no `to public` on either table, and a caller who is not signed in has `auth.uid()` NULL, which never satisfies a WHERE, so every policy denies. The `FOR INSERT ... WITH CHECK` is the half that matters and is asserted as present: without it a caller could INSERT a row naming another user and then read it back through the SELECT policy. Measured: user B's INSERT naming user A was rejected with `new row violates row-level security policy for table "user_news_preferences"`.

NO DELETE POLICY IS ADDED, DELIBERATELY, AND THAT IS A DECISION RATHER THAN AN OMISSION. The consumer never deletes, so granting delete would be an access grant with no caller behind it. Delete is therefore denied to every caller - measured: `ERROR: permission denied for table user_news_preferences` - which is the safe default for a table whose deletion semantics (unsubscribe-all? cascade from a subscriptions table? retain for ranking history?) nobody has specified. If the discover lane needs delete, it is one more `create policy ... for delete to authenticated using (auth.uid() = user_id)` and a decision about the data, not about the schema.

RLS is enabled AND FORCED on both tables. ENABLE alone leaves a hole: RLS is skipped for the table's OWNER, and these tables are owned by the migration role. FORCE closes it, following the chain's own convention (10 active migrations use `force row level security`, including 20260927100000 / 100100 / 100200 from the same day). It does not affect `service_role`, which has BYPASSRLS and is what an admin or fan-out path would use.

GRANTS ARE EXPLICIT TO `authenticated` ONLY, and `anon` is granted nothing. Supabase's default privileges normally cover a table created in `public`, but DB-013's harness failure was precisely a missing table grant turning an intended read into a functional FALSE-DENIAL, and a target with drifted defaults would reproduce it. An explicit grant is additive and names one role. The post-condition asserts `anon` holds no SELECT, measured green after a deliberate `grant select ... to anon` was made and the gate was run (see `evidence`).

NO TYPE REGENERATION IS NEEDED FOR THIS FILE AND NONE WAS DONE. `lib/database.types.ts` is byte-unchanged (SHA-256 168daaff01fb7ef285fb7bc69cfb5876cb092491953cdbbb2cea3fa7cb7558ab7). It declares NEITHER table today, which is correct: these tables do not exist. A chain-built regeneration (CP-127's verdict) will add both. Regeneration itself is blocked on RELEASE-013 provisioning a chain-built target and stays on DB-008 via HF-TICKET-006-DATABASE-TYPES.
layeredPlan: Layer 0 (preflight, read-only, operator). Run the rowCountQueries and record the result. Four things decide whether this file is correct for THIS target: (a) whether either table already exists - `create table if not exists` is a silent no-op against an existing relation, and the post-condition's relkind and unique-constraint checks are what catch a shape mismatch, but the operator should know before applying; (b) whether `authenticated` already holds the table grants this file issues, so a duplicate grant is expected and harmless; (c) that `anon` holds NOTHING on either name, which is the anonymity boundary the personalization signal depends on; (d) that `auth.users` and the `authenticated` / `anon` roles exist, which is a hard precondition of every statement in the file.

Layer 1 (apply, single run, operator). One transaction, explicit, this file only - never `supabase db reset`, never `db push --include-all`, never a chain replay (CP-051). Two `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS`, two `CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS`, four `ALTER TABLE ... ENABLE/FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY`, six `DROP POLICY IF EXISTS` + `CREATE POLICY` pairs, four `GRANT`s, then the post-condition DO block. The post-condition is inside the same transaction as the change, so a target that cannot reach the asserted state fails the apply rather than reporting success. Nothing here touches an existing relation, so there is no ordering constraint against any other migration and none against the other two DB-019 files.

Layer 2 (postflight, read-only, operator). Run the postflight queries, then the real-caller probes AS THE IDENTITIES NAMED. The whole point of this file is a read that used to return nothing, so the only proof is a read that now returns the caller's own rows and a write that now returns the caller's own row - and both must be run as two DIFFERENT signed-in accounts, because a single-identity probe cannot distinguish own-rows-only from see-everything.

Layer 3 (no fourth layer in this lane). Four items are routed rather than absorbed: the delete policy decision, the `updated_at` trigger (no caller writes these tables yet, and a trigger on a table with no writer is a mechanism with no use), the fan-out that would use `idx_user_news_subscriptions_type_key`, and CP-016 type regeneration. None is required for this file to be safe.

preflight.expectedAffectedRows: Two relations are CREATED, empty: `user_news_preferences` and `user_news_subscriptions`. Two indexes are created, two on tables that were just created and are empty, and three constraints per table come with the CREATE. RLS is enabled and forced on both. Six policies are created (three per table). Four grants are issued to `authenticated`. ZERO data rows are created, updated or deleted, because this migration creates the tables and no consumer writes them yet. If Layer 0 reports either table already existing, the CREATE is a no-op and the created-object list above applies only to the table that did not exist.

execution.resumeStrategy: Authored - manual apply pending (CP-051). One transaction, one file. Both tables are created empty in this migration, so there is no data lock to speak of: CREATE TABLE takes locks on catalog rows only, the two CREATE INDEX statements build over zero rows, and ENABLE/FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY and GRANT take catalog locks. The lock budget is therefore independent of any existing data volume, which is a property of creating tables rather than of the statements. Safe to apply in any order relative to the other two DB-019 files and to every other migration: this file touches no existing relation. Safe to apply BEFORE any consumer change: nothing reads these tables today, so no committed surface can change behaviour. The file is re-runnable, so a re-apply is a no-op rather than an error.
execution.idempotency: Deterministic and repeatable, verified by applying the file THREE times consecutively on a throwaway PostgreSQL 16.15 cluster: every apply exited 0 and the relation set, column set, constraint set, RLS flags, the exact six-name policy set and the post-condition result were identical after each. `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS`, `CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS`, `DROP POLICY IF EXISTS` + `CREATE POLICY` with a final name, and idempotent `GRANT` are each individually re-runnable.

quarantine.strategy: No data movement, no backfill, no batch, no quarantine table - both tables are created empty in this migration and nothing writes them yet. There is no partial-application state: the file is one transaction and its own post-condition RAISEs if the asserted state is unreachable, so a half-created table or a half-applied policy set cannot be committed. The only interesting partial state is a target where ONE of the two tables already existed out of band, and the post-condition's column, unique-constraint and policy-set assertions are what make that target fail the apply rather than half-succeed.
quarantine.lockBudget: No statement in this file scans or rewrites an existing table, so the lock cost is constant. The two indexes are built over zero rows. The post-condition's catalog reads (pg_class, pg_policy, pg_constraint, information_schema.columns) take ACCESS SHARE on catalog rows only and cannot queue behind a data lock.

constraints: ON public.user_news_preferences: primary key on `id`; `constraint user_news_preferences_user_id_key unique (user_id)`; NOT NULL on `user_id`, `topics`, `preferred_sources`, `created_at`; `user_id references auth.users(id) on delete cascade`. The unique constraint is load-bearing for the consumer, not hygiene - see `assumptions`.

ON public.user_news_subscriptions: primary key on `id`; `constraint user_news_subscriptions_type_check check (subscription_type in ('topic','source'))`; `constraint user_news_subscriptions_unique_key unique (user_id, subscription_type, subscription_key)`; NOT NULL on `user_id`, `subscription_type`, `subscription_key`, `created_at`; `user_id references auth.users(id) on delete cascade`.

ALL SIX are declared INLINE in the `CREATE TABLE` rather than as `ALTER TABLE ... ADD CONSTRAINT`. That is deliberate: `scripts/ci/check-migration-validation.mjs` flags a CHECK or FK added to an EXISTING table unless it is `NOT VALID` or carries a reviewed lock-budget marker, because validating a constraint on a populated table is the expensive operation. On a table created in the same statement there is nothing to scan and nothing to lock, and declaring them inline keeps the file free of the exception machinery.

`on delete cascade` on `user_id` means deleting an `auth.users` row removes that reader's preferences and subscriptions. That is the correct erasure semantics for personalisation data and is stated here because it is a deletion behaviour this file introduces, not inherits.
NO policy, grant or RLS setting on any OTHER relation is created, altered or dropped by this file. `artist_blog_posts` and `artist_music` are not touched at all.
indexes: `idx_user_news_subscriptions_user_created on public.user_news_subscriptions (user_id, created_at desc)` serves the consumer's actual query, `.eq('user_id', ...)` with no other filter, in the order a subscriptions list would be rendered. It is redundant with the `user_id` prefix of `user_news_subscriptions_unique_key` for pure filtering, and is kept for the ordered read the table will grow into.

`idx_user_news_subscriptions_type_key on public.user_news_subscriptions (subscription_type, subscription_key)` is for the INVERSE query - which readers follow this topic or source - which is the fan-out the personalization ranking will need and which NO current caller makes. It is cheap (one row per subscription) and is created now rather than at fan-out time so that adding fan-out does not arrive with an unindexed table. Recorded as anticipatory, not as covering a consumer.

NO index is added to `user_news_preferences` beyond the unique constraint's own index on `user_id`, which is the only access path the consumer has. A GIN index on `topics` would be the index for a topic-fan-out query and is deliberately NOT created: no caller makes one, and an unused GIN index on a table that grows per-reader is pure write amplification.
`ON public.artist_blog_posts` and `public.music_tracks` are NOT touched by this file.
constraintsAndIndexes.validationPlan: The file's own post-condition DO block is the target-side validation, and it is proven able to FAIL in the four ways that matter, measured by executing the extracted block standalone against a deliberately broken state: (1) with a seventh policy `USING (true)` added to `user_news_preferences` - the CP-104 shape - it raised on the scoping check; (2) with the INSERT policy's WITH CHECK replaced by `with check (true)`, it raised on the same check; (3) with `no force row level security` on `user_news_subscriptions` ONLY, it raised `RLS is not enabled AND forced on BOTH news preference tables; offenders: user_news_subscriptions`; (4) with `grant select ... to anon` issued, it raised `anon holds a SELECT grant on a news preference table`. Each was followed by a re-apply that returned it to GREEN. The block additionally asserts the relkind of both relations, the six consumer columns by name (reporting the first missing set rather than collapsing to a boolean), the structural unique constraint on `user_id`, and that no policy on either table is reachable by PUBLIC or anon. NO committed contract-test `.sql` file is provided: `supabase/tests/` is outside DB-019's working set, and the operator's Layer 2 queries plus this block are the target-side check.

recovery.rollback: `DROP TABLE IF EXISTS public.user_news_subscriptions; DROP TABLE IF EXISTS public.user_news_preferences;` issued as a LATER FORWARD MIGRATION, never as an edit to this file, and only after `SELECT count(*)` on both has been recorded - because a rollback DELETES every reader's stored personalization, which is real data even though no consumer writes it yet. Rolling back returns the target to exactly the state this task found: the tables absent, and `lib/news/feed-service.ts` reporting `preferences` as a degraded source. That is a truthful state, not a regression, because it is the state every deployed environment is in today. No policy, grant or RLS setting needs separate rollback: they go with the tables.
recovery.forwardFix: Any correction is a new additive migration with a higher version. Three shapes are already anticipated by this file's post-condition, so a bad forward fix cannot be applied silently: a policy set that is not exactly these six names, a policy whose clause does not carry `auth.uid() = user_id`, and RLS enabled but not forced on either table all RAISE. Adding the seventh policy (a DELETE policy) is the one legitimate forward fix that the current post-condition will REJECT, because it asserts a count of exactly 6; that is intended, and the forward fix must state the new expected count rather than relax the check.

queries: SELECT c.relname, c.relkind, c.relrowsecurity, c.relforcerowsecurity FROM pg_class c JOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid = c.relnamespace WHERE n.nspname = 'public' AND c.relname IN ('user_news_preferences','user_news_subscriptions') ORDER BY c.relname;

SELECT c.relname, p.polname, p.polcmd, p.polpermissive, p.polroles::regrole[], pg_get_expr(p.polqual, p.polrelid) AS using_expr, pg_get_expr(p.polwithcheck, p.polrelid) AS check_expr FROM pg_policy p JOIN pg_class c ON c.oid = p.polrelid JOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid = c.relnamespace WHERE n.nspname = 'public' AND c.relname IN ('user_news_preferences','user_news_subscriptions') ORDER BY c.relname, p.polcmd, p.polname;

SELECT table_name, column_name, data_type, is_nullable, column_default FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_schema = 'public' AND table_name IN ('user_news_preferences','user_news_subscriptions') ORDER BY table_name, column_name;

SELECT conrelid::regclass AS table_name, conname, contype, pg_get_constraintdef(oid) FROM pg_constraint WHERE conrelid IN ('public.user_news_preferences'::regclass, 'public.user_news_subscriptions'::regclass) ORDER BY 1, 2;

-- ANONYMITY BOUNDARY. Both must return false. A true here is a release blocker, not a tuning knob: these tables hold per-reader behaviour and an anonymous reader must not reach them. SELECT has_table_privilege('anon','public.user_news_preferences','select') AS anon_prefs, has_table_privilege('anon','public.user_news_subscriptions','select') AS anon_subs;

-- PROBE 1, as USER A with USER A's own JWT. Expect 1 row (or 0 if the reader has never set a preference), NOT an error. This is the query that used to be permanently empty. SELECT topics, preferred_sources FROM public.user_news_preferences WHERE user_id = auth.uid();

-- PROBE 2, as USER B with USER B's own JWT. Expect 0 rows and NO error. A `PGRST116 multiple (or no) rows returned` here means user_id is not unique and the .maybeSingle() in the consumer is unsafe. SELECT topics, preferred_sources FROM public.user_news_preferences WHERE user_id = auth.uid();
-- PROBE 3, the boundary, as USER B. Expect 0 rows: RLS must hide USER A's row rather than erroring. SELECT count(*) FROM public.user_news_preferences;

-- PROBE 4, fail-closed on write, as USER B. Expect `ERROR: new row violates row-level security policy for table "user_news_preferences"`. INSERT 0 1 is a FAILURE and means any signed-in user can write into any other user's preferences. INSERT INTO public.user_news_preferences (user_id, topics) VALUES ('<user A uuid>', ARRAY['probe']);

-- PROBE 5, anon. Expect `ERROR: permission denied for table user_news_preferences`. A 0-row result instead means anon holds a grant and RLS is the only thing standing between an anonymous caller and every reader's preferences. SELECT count(*) FROM public.user_news_preferences;

-- PROBE 6, the check constraint, as USER A. Expect `ERROR: new row ... violates check constraint "user_news_subscriptions_type_check"`; an accepted row is a FAILURE, because the consumer silently discards any type it does not recognise. INSERT INTO public.user_news_subscriptions (user_id, subscription_type, subscription_key) VALUES (auth.uid(), 'weekly_digest', 'probe');

-- PROBE 7, the unique constraint, as USER A. Expect `ERROR: duplicate key value violates unique constraint "user_news_subscriptions_unique_key"`; an accepted duplicate is a FAILURE, because the consumer folds subscriptions into a Set so a duplicate is invisible at the read and permanent in the table. INSERT INTO public.user_news_subscriptions (user_id, subscription_type, subscription_key) SELECT user_id, subscription_type, subscription_key FROM public.user_news_subscriptions LIMIT 1;
-- PROBE 8, delete is denied by design. Expect `ERROR: permission denied for table user_news_preferences`. DELETE FROM public.user_news_preferences WHERE user_id = auth.uid();

User B's unqualified read returns 0 rows, so RLS hides user A's row. User B's INSERT naming user A is REJECTED with `new row violates row-level security policy for table "user_news_preferences"`. THE POST-CONDITION IS PROVEN ABLE TO FAIL, FOUR TIMES, and each control was checked for vacuousness before being believed. (1) a seventh `USING (true)` policy - the CP-104 shape - raised on the scoping check; (2) the INSERT policy's WITH CHECK replaced by `with check (true)` raised on the same check; (3) `no force row level security` on ONE of the two tables raised, naming the offender; (4) `grant select ... to anon` raised. Each was followed by a re-apply that returned the block to GREEN.

TWO REAL DEFECTS IN THIS FILE WERE FOUND BY RUNNING IT, both in the post-condition, and both are the repository's own recurring instrument class rather than anything new. (1) The first draft asserted `p.polwithcheck is null` on every policy, which reports a HEALTHY `FOR SELECT` policy as a violation because a SELECT policy's WITH CHECK is structurally absent. That is precisely the polqual/polwithcheck confusion DB-013 and DB-014 each reintroduced in this same repository hours apart, and this file reintroduced it as well; the fix is to branch on `polcmd` across all four shapes - SELECT and DELETE have USING only, INSERT has WITH CHECK only, UPDATE and ALL have both. (2) The first draft asserted RLS with `EXISTS (... AND relname IN (...))`, which returns true as soon as ONE of the two tables is correct, so `no force row level security` on exactly one of them read GREEN. It was rewritten as a COUNT of 2 that names the offender. Both were caught by running the file against a deliberately broken state, not by reading it, which is the only reason either was caught at all.
